learn.hook: Every gadget you use — from a pencil sharpener to a mobile phone — began as someone's 'crazy' idea!
points: 'My Brother's Great Invention' is a lesson about a sibling who keeps creating things. Here is our own story on the theme.
To invent is to make something new that did not exist before.
To discover is to find something that already existed but was not known: C. V. Raman discovered the Raman effect in 1928.
Inventors are curious, creative and patient; each failure shows them how to improve.
Word family: invent (verb), invention (noun), inventor (person), inventive (adjective).

example.q: Read: My brother Kunal tied an old umbrella, two spoons and a toy motor together. "Behold the Mango-Picker 3000!" he announced. The machine wobbled, buzzed and shook the branch — and one ripe mango dropped straight onto his head. Kunal rubbed his head and grinned. "Version two will have a basket," he said. What does 'Version two will have a basket' show about Kunal?
steps: The machine shook the mango loose, but it fell on his head — a small failure.
Kunal grins instead of getting upset.
He already plans an improvement: a basket to catch the mango.
example.answer: He learns from his mistake and plans to improve his invention — he is creative and does not give up.

learn.reallife: India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the day in 1928 when C. V. Raman announced his discovery.

games.title: Invented or discovered?
items: a new star in the sky

games.title: How inventors work
items: Think of ideas to solve it.

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'Kunal ___ a new machine from old spoons and a motor.'
quiz.explain: He made something new that did not exist before, so he invented it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up invent and discover

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'Scientists have ___ a new kind of frog in the Western Ghats.'
quiz.explain: The frog already existed in nature; scientists found it, so they discovered it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything new to us is 'invented'

quiz.q: A person who invents things is called an:
quiz.explain: Inventor is the person; invention is the thing made; inventive is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Confuses forms in the same word family

quiz.q: What does 'inventive' mean?
options: creative and good at thinking of new ideas
quiz.explain: An inventive person comes up with new, clever ideas.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the adjective with 'invent'

quiz.q: '"Behold the Mango-Picker 3000!" he announced.' Here 'announced' means:
options: said loudly and proudly to everyone
quiz.explain: To announce is to tell people something publicly, often with pride.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a meaning that does not fit the exclamation mark

quiz.q: 'The machine wobbled, buzzed and shook the branch — and one ripe mango dropped straight onto his head.' What happened?
options: A mango fell on Kunal's head
quiz.explain: The machine shook the branch, and the mango dropped onto his head.
quiz.mistake: Adds events that are not in the text

quiz.q: 'Kunal rubbed his head and grinned. "Version two will have a basket."' This shows Kunal is:
quiz.explain: He smiles and plans a better version — he learns from the failure.
quiz.mistake: Misses the clue 'grinned' and his new plan

quiz.q: Which day in India celebrates C. V. Raman's discovery of the Raman effect?
quiz.explain: National Science Day is celebrated on 28 February, the day Raman announced his discovery in 1928.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up national days

teach.ask: Gappu says his cousin 'discovered' a new paper-plane design. Is that the right word? Explain invent and discover.
teach.praise: Got it! My cousin invented the plane design — but I discovered a hidden worm!
teach.nudge: Which word is for making something new, and which is for finding something that already exists?

learn.hook: One tiny mark — the apostrophe — tells you whether the robot belongs to one brother or to three!
points: Siblings are brothers and sisters. Friendly competition between them is called sibling rivalry.
To show that something belongs to one person, add 's: my brother's invention.
For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: my brothers' room (two or more brothers).
For a plural noun not ending in s, add 's: the children's toys, the women's team.
Its = belonging to it (The cat licked its paw). It's = it is (It's raining).

example.q: I have one sister. Is it 'my sisters' bicycle' or 'my sister's bicycle'?
steps: Only one sister owns the bicycle → singular noun.
For a singular noun we add 's.

learn.reallife: Name boards like 'Sharma's Sweets' or 'Children's Park' use apostrophes to show who something belongs to.

games.title: Family words
pairs: daughter of your brother or sister
son of your brother or sister
child of your aunt or uncle

items.text: The two ___ kites flew high. (two girls)
The ___ room is full of toys. (children)

quiz.q: One brother owns the robot. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: For one owner, add 's to the noun: brother's.
quiz.mistake: Puts the apostrophe after the s for a single owner

quiz.q: Three sisters share a room. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: 'Sisters' is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe: sisters'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the singular form for many owners

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'the ___ playground'
quiz.explain: 'Children' is already plural and doesn't end in s, so we add 's.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s to 'children' as if it were singular

quiz.q: What does 'siblings' mean?
quiz.explain: Siblings are children of the same parents.
quiz.mistake: Confuses siblings with other relatives

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'The cat licked ___ paw.'
quiz.explain: 'Its' shows belonging. 'It's' means 'it is', which doesn't fit here.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every possessive needs an apostrophe

quiz.q: Choose the right word: '___ raining, so take an umbrella.'
quiz.explain: We mean 'It is raining', so the short form is 'It's'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up its and it's

quiz.q: What does 'sibling rivalry' mean?
options: a game played only by cousins
quiz.explain: Rivalry means competition; sibling rivalry is when brothers and sisters compete.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word 'rivalry'

quiz.q: Your father's sister is your:
quiz.explain: Your parent's sister is your aunt.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up family relationships

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 'my brothers invention' about his ONE brother. Where should the apostrophe go?
teach.praise: Oh! 'My brother's invention' — the apostrophe shows it belongs to my one brother!
teach.nudge: Where does the apostrophe go, and what does it show?

learn.hook: Even a great inventor needs clear steps — or the machine ends up upside down!
points: Instructions tell how to make or do something, step by step.
They use imperative sentences — commands or requests that usually begin with a verb: 'Cut the paper.' The subject 'you' is understood.
Sequence words show order: first, next, then, after that, finally.
A list of materials (things needed) comes before the steps.
Other kinds of sentences: assertive (statement), interrogative (question) and exclamatory (strong feeling).

example.q: Write instructions for making nimbu pani (lemonade).
steps: Materials: a glass of water, one lemon, sugar, a pinch of salt.
First, squeeze the lemon into the water.
Next, add sugar and a pinch of salt.
example.answer: First squeeze the lemon, next add sugar and salt, then stir, and finally serve.

learn.reallife: Recipe books, game rules, medicine labels and model kits all use imperative sentences and sequence words.

games.title: Make nimbu pani
items: Squeeze half a lemon into it.
Add sugar and a pinch of salt.

quiz.q: Which is an imperative sentence?
quiz.explain: It gives a command and begins with the verb 'fold'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence about a task is imperative

quiz.q: In 'Stir the mixture well', who is the understood subject?
quiz.explain: Imperative sentences speak to the listener, so 'you' is understood.
quiz.mistake: Thinks imperatives have no subject at all

quiz.q: Which word best begins the last step of instructions?
quiz.explain: 'Finally' signals the last step.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the order of sequence words

quiz.q: 'Please shut the door.' What kind of sentence is this?
quiz.explain: It is a polite request or command, so it is imperative.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'please' makes it a question

quiz.q: 'What a clever invention!' What kind of sentence is this?
quiz.explain: It shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'What' always begins a question

quiz.q: 'Did your brother build this?' What kind of sentence is this?
quiz.explain: It asks a question and ends with a question mark.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sentence types

quiz.q: In written instructions, what usually comes before the steps?
quiz.explain: We first list what is needed, then give the steps.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the format of instructions

quiz.q: Choose the word to begin this step: '___ the seeds in wet cotton and keep them in a warm place.'
quiz.explain: Imperative steps begin with the base form of the verb: 'Put'.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s or -ing to the verb in a command

teach.ask: Gappu wants to tell his friend how to build a nest. How should he write the instructions?
teach.praise: First, collect twigs. Next, weave them... I can write instructions now!
teach.nudge: What kind of word should each step begin with, and how do we show the order?
